Cassio. The young officer in Shakespeare's Othello whose innocence becomes the linchpin of the tragedy. Iago falsely accuses Cassio of an affair with Desdemona, using this lie to poison Othello's mind and destroy three lives. Cassio survives the play, but only after witnessing the catastrophe his false reputation unleashed.

Cassio is Othello's promising young lieutenant, promoted to a position of authority that Iago bitterly covets. This makes him Iago's immediate target for systematic destruction and humiliation. Iago deliberately intoxicates Cassio, provokes him into a drunken fight with Roderigo, and cynically uses the incident to convince Othello that Cassio is morally unfit for command and an adulterer.

The accusation that Cassio has been intimate with Desdemona is entirely fabricated. Iago invents it from nothing, manipulating circumstantial evidence and Othello's profound susceptibility to racist suspicion and jealousy. Cassio's actual courtship of Desdemona is blameless and formally respectful. His only genuine fault is his youth, his pride in his position, and his tragic susceptibility to Iago's manipulation.

His horror at being publicly disgraced and shamed, and his desperate attempts to restore his ruined reputation, contrast sharply with Iago's ice-cold cruelty and highlight the human cost of false accusation. Cassio emerges as the primary surviving witness to the tragedy, spared by Othello's final act of violence, yet psychologically devastated by his role in events and powerless to prevent catastrophe. The pattern of Cassio's destruction reveals how reputation, once corrupted, becomes unrecoverable despite innocence—a meditation on the fragility of social standing and masculine honor in Venice.
